images.after: Step 2: Set a pace you can keep for six months
images.title: Work out a pace from your hours
images.alt: Three steps for setting a posting pace: time one finished article, count your weekly hours, then divide and plan for about three quarters.
images.caption: Plan from the hours you actually have, not a number that sounds ambitious.

items.title: Time one finished article
items.text: Include research, editing, images and publishing. Time your next one if you don't know.

items.title: Count your weekly hours
items.text: Only the hours a week you can reliably give the blog.

items.title: Divide, then plan for 3/4
items.text: Plan for about three quarters of the result. The spare quarter covers weeks that go wrong.

images.note: Example: six hours a week at about five hours per article is roughly one a week

images.after: Pillar first, or supporting posts first?
images.title: Pillar first or supporting posts first?
images.alt: Decision chart: on a new site publish two or three supporting posts before the pillar; if you know the topic well, the pillar can go first.
images.caption: Either order works, because internal links can be added after the fact.

data.question: Do you already know the topic well?

branches.result: Publish two or three supporting posts first. Put the pillar by slot four or five.
Pillar first is fine too. Schedule a "links to add" task for each new post.

images.after: Step 5: Reserve slots for updating old posts
images.title: What counts as an update
images.alt: Comparison of a real update, which corrects facts, fills gaps and replaces stale examples, with a date-only change Google lists as a warning sign.
images.caption: Give updates a recurring slot. One a month is a reasonable start.

columns.label: A date-only change
points: Done to make the page seem fresh
Google lists it as a warning sign
